analysis.one_liner: Charges hardrock miners an 8% royalty and cleanup bonds and shields sensitive federal lands from new mining claims.
analysis.headline: With 39 cosponsors, the bill got one subcommittee hearing in February 2009, then sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the General Mining Law of 1872, companies can stake claims on federal land and take gold, silver, copper, and other hardrock minerals without paying any royalty to the government, and in some cases buy the land outright. This bill would charge an 8% royalty on new production (4% on mines already operating), require operating permits backed by cleanup bonds, close wilderness study areas and roadless forests to new claims, and let states, local governments, and Indian tribes petition to shield specific federal lands, such as drinking-water watersheds, from mining. The money collected would go into a fund to clean up abandoned mines and help the towns and tribes affected by mining.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently foot the bill for cleaning up abandoned hardrock mines and receive no royalty on minerals taken from their land; communities downstream of abandoned mines, whose waters would be protected and whose contaminated sites would become eligible for cleanup funding; Indian tribes and local governments, which would gain a formal way to petition to protect culturally or economically important lands; and small claim holders, who are exempted from the new maintenance fee.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Subjects hardrock mining on federal claims to a royalty of 8% of gross income from mining, with a reduced 4% rate for mines already operating under a permit, and deposits the proceeds in a public fund.

Requires operators to post financial assurance — a bond, trust fund, or equivalent — covering the full cost of reclamation and, where needed, long-term water treatment, so cleanup does not fall to the government if a company walks away.
Closes wilderness study areas, areas of critical environmental concern, inventoried roadless areas, and Wild and Scenic River study areas to new mining claims.

Lets any state, local government, or Indian tribe petition the Interior Secretary to withdraw a specific tract of federal land from mining to protect values like drinking-water watersheds, wildlife habitat, or tribal cultural and religious sites, with a decision due within 180 days.

Creates a Locatable Minerals Fund fed by royalties, fees, and penalties, split two-thirds to reclaim abandoned mine lands and waters and one-third to assist states, towns, and tribes economically affected by mining.
Effectively ends the practice of patenting mining claims — obtaining title to federal land for a nominal payment — by limiting new patents to applications already filed by September 30, 1994.
Bars companies (and their affiliates) with unresolved environmental violations from receiving mining permits.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies, which would for the first time pay royalties, annual claim fees, and the full cost of cleanup bonds on federal-land operations. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through mineral prices, and industry backers warned the requirements could reduce domestic production of minerals used in electronics and defense. Small claimants holding ten or fewer claims are spared the annual fee if they perform the old assessment work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gold, silver, and copper mining companies

drawbacks.text: The 8% royalty and full-cost bonding would raise operating expenses for an industry that historically paid none, and opponents argued this could shrink domestic production of minerals the economy depends on and cost jobs in mining towns — a concern the bill partly addresses by routing one-third of the fund to assist mining-affected communities.

Existing operations are largely grandfathered: mines already producing pay only a 4% royalty, and claims with approved operating plans can continue under the old rules for up to ten years, delaying reform at precisely the sites already causing environmental damage.
Cleanup of abandoned mines depends on annual appropriations from the new fund, so reclamation of the hundreds of thousands of legacy sites would proceed only as money accumulates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on an industry that currently takes hardrock minerals from federal land without paying a royalty and has often left taxpayers the cleanup bill; the benefits — royalty revenue, cleaner watersheds, and a dedicated abandoned-mine fund — go to the public. The grandfathering of existing mines and the 4% rate for current operations are real compromises that soften the bill's effect, but the core trade favors the public side of the ledger.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in January 2009 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, the bill got one subcommittee hearing that February, but was never brought to a committee vote or the House floor, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Rahall of West Virginia introduced the bill on January 27, 2009, and it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which he chaired.
Thirty-nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.
On February 4, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, which held a hearing on February 26, 2009.
No further action appears in the record: the bill was never marked up in committee, never received a floor vote, and expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: they kept taking gold, silver, and copper from federal land without paying royalties or posting full-cost cleanup bonds, and taxpayers continued to bear the cost of cleaning up abandoned mine sites.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies that kept royalty-free access

for.name: Rep. Nick Rahall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his committee, where its only hearing was held; the bill never advanced to a markup or floor vote.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: National Mining Association and allied mining companies
against.what_they_did: Opposed hardrock mining reform legislation that would impose royalties and reclamation requirements on federal-land mining.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 members who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Democrats; because no vote was ever taken, no opposition lineup was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, silver, copper, uranium)
industries.note: These companies currently pay no royalty on minerals taken from federal land under the 1872 mining law and often leave cleanup costs to taxpayers. The bill would impose an 8% royalty on new production, 4% on existing mines, annual claim fees, and full-cost cleanup bonds — a direct hit to an industry whose gain under the status quo comes at the public's expense.

industries.industry: Small prospectors and small claim holders
industries.note: Claimants holding ten or fewer claims are exempted from the new annual maintenance fee if they keep doing assessment work, but they would still face permitting, royalty, and bonding requirements like larger operators.
